issues.legal_issue: A law providing for state-appointed administration of endowed property does not infringe a religious denomination’s right to administer that property when the denomination never held that right.
material_facts: The endowment’s property was managed by officials appointed by the government, who were answerable to it, from the time substantial endowments began.
The denomination had never managed the endowed property, and the shrine’s visitors and beneficiaries were not confined to that denomination or to Muslims.
The petition challenged the statutory committee’s administration of the endowment on the ground that the denomination was entitled to manage it.
issues.conclusion: The challenged provisions establishing the committee and vesting administration and management of the endowment in it did not violate Article 26(c) or (d).
issues.legal_principle: Article 26(c) and (d) safeguard and continue rights a denomination or section already had; they do not create a right to administer property that it never held, surrendered, or otherwise irretrievably lost. Article 26 protection is confined to practices that are essential and integral parts of religion. The Court discussed Commissioner, Hindu Religious Endowments, Madras v. Sri Lakshmindra Thirtha Swamiar of Sri Shirur Mutt, [1954] S.C.R. 1005, and Sri Venkataramana Devaru v. The State of Mysore, [1958] S.C.R. 895, and relied on the historical account and Asrar Ahmed v. Durgah Committee, Ajmer, A.I.R. 1947 P.C. 1.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_endowment_ma: A party challenged a law that provides for administration and management of an endowment.
predicates.denomination_claims_control_of_endowed_p: A religious denomination or section claimed that it was entitled to manage the endowed property.
predicates.state_appointees_managed_endowment: Officials appointed by the state managed the endowment and were answerable to the state.
predicates.denomination_never_managed_endowment: The denomination or section had never managed the endowed property.

issues.definition: When a denomination challenges an endowment-management law, its claim to manage the property does not defeat the law if state appointees managed it and the denomination never did.

issues.legal_issue: Rules assigning to the institution offerings earmarked for it, and authorising its representative to solicit and receive those offerings, do not infringe the claimants’ property rights when those offerings were not theirs under the established allocation of offerings.
material_facts: Earlier judicial decisions recognised that offerings intended for the general purposes of the shrine belonged to the shrine, while other offerings could belong to the Khadims or the Sajjadanashin.
The challenged provisions included offerings received on behalf of the shrine in its endowment and authorised the Nazim or an authorised person to solicit and receive offerings on its behalf.
The Act did not prevent pilgrims from making offerings to the Khadims, who could accept offerings made to them.
issues.conclusion: The definition of the endowment and the provision authorising the Nazim or his agent to solicit and receive offerings on behalf of the institution did not violate Article 19(1)(f) or (g).
issues.legal_principle: Articles 19(1)(f) and (g) did not invalidate rules concerning property belonging to the institution. Offerings earmarked generally for the institution belonged to it, and the legislature could regulate who solicited or received them. The Court relied on the earlier decisions, particularly Syed Altaf Hussain v. Dewan Syed Ali Rasul Ali Khan, A.I.R. 1938 P.C. 71, and held that the challenged provisions did not take from the claimants offerings recognised as theirs.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_institutiona: A party challenged rules governing offerings received on behalf of an institution.
predicates.offerings_were_earmarked_for_institution: The offerings at issue were made or received for the institution’s general purposes.
predicates.prior_judicial_findings_allocated_such_o: Earlier judicial decisions treated offerings of that kind as belonging to the institution rather than to the claimants.
predicates.claimants_could_still_accept_offerings_m: The rules did not prevent the claimants from accepting offerings that visitors made to them.

issues.definition: The institutional offerings rules do not infringe the claimants’ property rights when the offerings were earmarked for the institution, earlier decisions allocated them to it, and the claimants could still accept offerings made to them.

issues.legal_issue: Regulation of the duties and functions of religious attendants and a spiritual officeholder does not infringe freedom of religion when the regulating body must observe the applicable religious law and tenets.
material_facts: The challenged provisions authorised the committee to determine the Khadims’ privileges and regulate their presence, and to determine any functions and powers of the Sajjadanashin in relation to the shrine.
The Khadims performed duties by rotation, making regulation of their discharge necessary.
The Act required the committee to observe Muslim law and the tenets of the Chishti saint when conducting and regulating established rites and ceremonies.
issues.conclusion: The challenged provisions did not violate Article 25(1).
issues.legal_principle: Article 25(1) protects freedom of conscience and the freedom to profess, practise, and propagate religion, but the powers at issue regulated the discharge of duties and functions rather than prohibiting religious practice. The provisions had to be read together with the Act’s mandatory requirement to observe Muslim law and the saint’s tenets. The Court’s discussion of essential and integral religious practices was consistent with Commissioner, Hindu Religious Endowments, Madras v. Sri Lakshmindra Thirtha Swamiar of Sri Shirur Mutt, [1954] S.C.R. 1005, and Sri Venkataramana Devaru v. The State of Mysore, [1958] S.C.R. 895.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_regulation_o: A party challenged a law regulating the duties of attendants and the functions of a religious officeholder.
predicates.attendants_performed_duties_by_rotation: The attendants carried out their duties by rotation.
predicates.regulating_body_was_required_to_observe_: The law required the regulating body to observe the applicable religious law and the institution’s religious tenets.

issues.definition: Regulation of attendants and officeholders does not infringe freedom of religion when their duties are performed by rotation and the regulating body must observe the applicable religious law and tenets.

issues.legal_issue: A statutory arbitration process for non-religious disputes between an institution’s managing body and its attendants does not infringe equality or the right to constitutional remedies when it provides for representation of both sides and an impartial qualified member.
material_facts: The Act referred disputes between the committee and the Khadims or other specified persons to a board of arbitration, except disputes concerning religious usage, custom, or the performance of religious office.
Each side nominated a member of the board, and a qualified person appointed by the government served as the third member.
The Act made the award final and barred a separate suit on a matter required to be referred to arbitration.
issues.conclusion: The arbitration provision did not violate Articles 14 or 32.
issues.legal_principle: A requirement of arbitration for non-religious disputes is not, by itself, contrary to Articles 14 or 32. The Court considered the provision a fair and sensible means of resolving disputes in the interests of the institution and the parties, while religious disputes remained outside its scope and could be determined through the ordinary law and competent civil courts.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_statutory_ar: A party challenged a law requiring arbitration of disputes between an institution’s managing body and specified persons connected with it.
predicates.arbitration_was_limited_to_nonreligious_: The arbitration process excluded disputes concerning religious usage, custom, or the performance of religious office.
predicates.each_side_nominated_an_arbitrator: Each side to a covered dispute nominated a member of the arbitration board.
predicates.an_impartial_qualified_member_completed_: A qualified and impartial third member completed the arbitration board.

issues.definition: A statutory arbitration process for institutional disputes does not infringe equality or constitutional remedies when it covers only non-religious disputes, each side nominates a member, and an impartial qualified member completes the board.

issues.legal_issue: A provision for interim arrangements when a religious office becomes vacant does not infringe freedom of religion when it forms part of a procedure for determining succession to that office.
material_facts: The challenged provision authorised the committee to make provisional arrangements for performing the functions of the Sajjadanashin when that office fell vacant.
The same statutory section prescribed the procedure for inviting applications and determining succession to the office.
issues.conclusion: The interim-arrangement provision did not violate Article 25(1).
issues.legal_principle: The interim-arrangement provision must be read with the rest of the section, whose principal purpose was to prescribe a procedure for determining succession. A temporary arrangement pending selection of a successor does not, on that reading, interfere with freedom of religion.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_interim_arra: A party challenged a law authorising temporary arrangements for the functions of a religious office.
predicates.interim_arrangements_were_part_of_a_succ: The temporary arrangements were provided within a procedure for determining a permanent successor.

issues.definition: Temporary arrangements for a vacant religious office do not infringe freedom of religion when they form part of a procedure for selecting a permanent successor.

issues.legal_issue: Enforcing a managing body’s final orders as civil court orders does not infringe equality or the right to constitutional remedies when the orders are within its jurisdiction and the affected persons did not object but failed to comply.
material_facts: The Act provided for enforcement of the committee’s final orders in the same manner as orders or decrees of a civil court.
The Court construed the provision as applying only to final orders within the committee’s jurisdiction and to persons who did not object to the orders but failed to comply.
Disputed non-religious matters were subject to arbitration, while religious matters were to be determined under ordinary law in competent civil courts.
issues.conclusion: The enforcement provision did not violate Articles 14 or 32.
issues.legal_principle: Read in context, the enforcement provision applied only to final orders within the committee’s jurisdiction that had not been objected to but had not been obeyed. Disputed matters were otherwise subject to the designated arbitration process or ordinary civil courts, so the provision did not offend equality or the right to constitutional remedies.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_enforcement_: A party challenged a law that allows a managing body’s orders to be enforced as civil court orders.
predicates.order_was_final_and_within_the_body_juri: The order was final and concerned a matter within the managing body’s jurisdiction.
predicates.affected_person_did_not_object_but_faile: The person against whom the order was made did not object to it but failed to comply.

issues.definition: Enforcement of a managing body’s order does not infringe equality or constitutional remedies when the order is final and within the body’s jurisdiction and the affected person did not object but failed to comply.
